sentences.text: This animal belongs to the sebecosuchian group within the notosuchian family.
The defining specimen is a slender lower jaw bone measuring exactly 156 mm in length.
The two halves of this jaw diverged by 10 to 15 degrees, reaching a height of at least 50 mm near the fourth tooth.
Its surface shows grooves and pits, while the surangular bone expands upward before thinning near the angular bone.
Fossils were found in 1982 at the El Kohol site in northern Algeria by teams from the Université d'Oran, Sorbonne Universités, and Université de Montpellier.
Buffetaut first described the species in 1989 using isolated skull and body parts.
It possessed serrated, blade-like teeth known as ziphodonty.
Changes in tooth shape from young to adult stages might indicate a shift in how it fed.
A gap between the seventh and eighth teeth in the juvenile could be a shared trait or just individual variation.
The scientific name is Eremosuchus, with the type species designated as E. elkoholicus.
It remains the only named sebecid known from Africa.
Analysis suggests it is closely related to South American land-dwelling sebecids, though these results are not fully conclusive.
This creature lived during the Ypresian stage of the Early Eocene.
As the sole named sebecid from continental Africa, it may connect South American and European groups.
Scientists debate whether its lineage split during sebecid dispersal between South America and Europe, or if ancestors moved from Europe to North Africa via the Tethys Sea.
Variation in tooth enamel ornamentation might represent individual or species-level differences rather than distinct species.
It is unclear if multiple osteoderm ornamentation types belong to this species or if neither type does.
Turner and Calvo argued that features used to assign it to Trematochampsidae hold questionable value.
